title: Migration cutover stability playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook describes the operational steps, monitoring, and escalation paths to ensure a stable migration/cutover for enterprise customers moving traffic to Redwood (Hosted / Dedicated / Private). It is intended for Customer Success, SRE, and the customer's technical owners. The document covers pre-cutover validation, immediate cutover actions (0–2 hours), degradation thresholds and automated mitigations, rollback criteria, and the 72-hour stabilization window.

When to use

- Planned migrations from another provider or self-hosted inference to Redwood Dedicated or Private.
- Large traffic shifts (>= 50% traffic change) or model variant swaps for production customers.
- Post-contract go-lives where SLAs and cost constraints are in effect.

Key goals

- Maintain SLOs: p95 latency < 500 ms (generation endpoints), error rate < 0.5% (5xx + client failures), embedding throughput within agreed baseline.
- Detect and contain regressions within 5–15 minutes.
- Provide deterministic rollback when criteria are exceeded.

Stakeholders and primary contacts

- Customer Success (primary owner): Aisha Patel (lead) — oncall: +1-415-555-0172, pager: @cs-oncall
- SRE/Platform: Carlos Rivera — slack: #sre-redwood, pager: @sre-oncall
- Serving Runtime Lead: Sophie Nguyen — slack: @sophie-nguyen
- Customer Technical Contact: (populate from onboarding worksheet) — recommended escalation cadence included below

Pre-cutover checklist (complete 72–1 hours before cutover)

1. Configuration & access
   - Confirm API keys and IP allowlists are provisioned. Example allowed CIDR list for customer egress: 10.2.0.0/16, 198.51.100.0/24.
   - If Private: validate VPC peering and firewall rules; test TCP handshake to inference endpoints (TLS 443).

2. Capacity & model readiness
   - Ensure dedicated capacity pool size matches forecasted TPS + 30% buffer. Documented in order: gpu-pool-size and expected token/sec.
   - Model variant pinned for cutover (model-id, quantization profile, kernel tag).

3. Test plan and synthetic traffic
   - Prepare a synthetic traffic generator with representative prompt mixes (short/long sequences, embeddings, chat). Sample CLI:

   rcli simulate traffic --target https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate --concurrency 50 --profile enterprise-cutover.json

   - Validate KV cache priming: run warmup scripts that exercise common prefixes and expected session lengths.

4. Observability preps
   - Create a cutover dashboard (p90/p95/p99 latency, error rate, request rate, GPU util, queue depth per pool).
   - Ensure tracing is enabled for customer requests; add sample span tag customer_id and route.

Immediate cutover steps (0–2 hours)

1. Communicate T-0 to stakeholders (status channel, customer contact).
2. Switch routing: update traffic router (or DNS) to send 10% of traffic to Redwood for 10 minutes, then 50% for 15 minutes, then 100% if green (recommended gradual ramp).
3. During each ramp phase execute checklist:
   - Verify p95 latency remains < 500 ms.
   - Verify error rate < 0.5%.
   - Confirm no queue depth exceeding threshold (see Alert thresholds table below).

Monitoring and health indicators

Primary metrics (track in dashboard):
- request.rate (rps) — baseline and delta
- request.p95_latency_ms — target < 500 ms
- request.error_rate_percent — target < 0.5%
- gpu.utilization_percent — avoid sustained > 90% for more than 5 minutes
- serving.queue_depth — alert when > 250 requests in queue per pool
- kv_cache.hit_rate_percent — expected > 70% after warmup for session-heavy apps

Alert thresholds (recommended)

| Alert name | Trigger | Severity | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| High error rate | error_rate_percent > 1.5% for 2m | P1 | Consider immediate rollback if sustained |
| Latency spike | p95_latency_ms > 1200 for 3m | P1 | Investigate model or kernel bottleneck |
| Queue saturation | queue_depth > 500 for 5m | P1 | Autoscale/limit ingestion; see mitigations |
| GPU saturation | gpu.utilization_percent > 95% for 10m | P2 | Trigger capacity expansion/eviction policies |
| KV cache missstorm | kv_cache.hit_rate_percent < 30% for 10m | P2 | May indicate warmup needed or routing mix issue |

Degradation behavior and automated mitigations

- For minor degradation (error_rate 0.5%–1.5% or p95 500–1200 ms): automatically throttle non-critical requests, reduce batch size, and enable fallback model variant with smaller footprint.
- For severe degradation (error_rate > 1.5% or sustained queue_depth > 500): engage rollback to previous provider routing or previous model version.
- Built-in automated actions (what Redwood platform can perform):
  - route.rebalance --move 50% traffic to fallback pool
  - model.variant_switch --to model-id:golden-small-quant

Rollback criteria and procedure

Rollback should be considered when ANY of the following are true for 10 minutes:
- request.error_rate_percent > 2.0% AND increasing
- p95_latency_ms > 1500 ms AND user impact confirmed
- queue_depth > 800 or sustained GPU OOM errors

Rollback steps (execute in order)
1. Notify stakeholders: open a migration incident and ping P1 channels.
2. Execute route rollback: revert routing to previous provider or traffic mirror. Command example:

   rcli traffic update --route customer-123 --percent 0 --target previous-provider

3. If rollback is to a previous model version in Redwood:

   rcli model promote --customer customer-123 --model-id "model-v1-stable"

4. Scale down any warm pool to reduce cost and surface residual errors for investigation.

Escalation matrix and communication

- Phase 0 (informal): Customer Success lead + customer tech contact (first 5 minutes).
- Phase 1 (operational): Add SRE and Serving Runtime lead (10–30 minutes).
- Phase 2 (critical): Engage Engineering on-call, Platform PM, SOC if security incident suspected (>30 minutes).

Contact table (primary means)
- Customer Success lead: Aisha Patel — slack: @aisha-patel, cell: +1-415-555-0172
- SRE oncall: Carlos Rivera — pager: @sre-oncall, slack: #sre-redwood
- Runtime lead: Sophie Nguyen — slack DM or escalation channel #runtime-oncall

Post-cutover stabilization (2–72 hours)

- Hours 2–6: Keep traffic at production level while running heavy monitoring. Run daily regression checks against representative prompt set (n=5000).
- 6–24 hours: Execute sample customer transactions end-to-end with logging enabled. Pay special attention to stateful chat sessions and embedding index builds.
- 24–72 hours: Prepare a stabilization report with metrics and anomalies; schedule a review with the customer to confirm SLA satisfaction and plan any follow-up mitigations.

Operational runbook snippets

- Check p95 for the last 10 minutes:

   rcli metrics query --service inference --customer customer-123 --metric request.p95_latency_ms --range 10m

- Promote fallback model (example JSON payload):

   {
     "customer_id": "customer-123",
     "action": "promote_model",
     "model_id": "model-v1-stable"
   }

- Quick health summary (one-liner for status channel):

   cutover-status: green | p95=320ms | errs=0.12% | gpu=48% | qd=42

Postmortem and RCA guidance

- If an incident occurs that required rollback or manual mitigation, create a postmortem within 72 hours. The postmortem should include: timeline, contributing factors, detection method, impact, remediation, and follow-up actions owners with SLAs (30 days for code fixes, 90 days for capacity changes).

Appendices

Appendix A — Example warmup script (bash):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
for i in {1..200}; do
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -d '{"prompt":"Summary of user event ${i}","max_tokens":64}' >/dev/null &
 done
wait
